subject: bio
title: Gas Exchange
subtitle: Gas exchange surfaces in mammals, fish, insects and plants.
concept: Efficient gas exchange requires: large surface area, thin surface, steep concentration gradient, and (in larger organisms) a ventilation mechanism.
Mammalian lungs maximise surface area with alveoli; the alveolar wall is one cell thick to minimise diffusion distance.
Insects use a tracheal system; fish use counter-current flow in gills; plants use stomata.

notes.heading: Features of Gas Exchange Surfaces
items: Large surface area: increases rate of diffusion.
Good blood supply / ventilation: maintains steep concentration gradient.

notes.heading: Mammalian Lungs
items: Ventilation: intercostal muscles + diaphragm change thorax volume → pressure changes → air moves in/out.
Inspiration: external intercostals contract, diaphragm contracts and flattens → volume increases → pressure falls → air in.
Expiration: internal intercostals + elastic recoil → volume decreases → pressure rises → air out.
Alveoli: ~700 million; lined with surfactant (prevents collapse); surrounded by capillaries; one-cell-thick squamous epithelium.
Fick's law: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness.

notes.heading: Fish Gills
items: Lamellae on gill arches; secondary lamellae provide large SA.
Counter-current flow: blood and water flow in opposite directions → concentration gradient maintained across entire gill → greater O₂ extraction (~80%) vs parallel flow (~50%).

notes.heading: Insects: Tracheal System
items: Air enters through spiracles (can be opened/closed to reduce water loss).
Tracheae divide into tracheoles → carry O₂ directly to cells.
No haemoglobin needed; relies on diffusion (only efficient in small organisms).
Spiracles close during rest to reduce water loss.

notes.heading: Plants: Stomata
items: CO₂ enters; O₂ and water vapour exit through stomata.
Guard cells: swell (turgid) to open stoma when water enters by osmosis; become flaccid to close.
Stomata usually open in daytime (photosynthesis demand); close at night and in water stress.
Xerophytes: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled leaves, stomata on lower surface — reduce water loss.

definitions.body: Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) / diffusion distance.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions across fish gills, maintaining a concentration gradient along the entire gill length.
Small opening in the exoskeleton of an insect through which air enters the tracheal system.
A pair of cells surrounding a stoma that control its opening and closing by changes in turgor.

workedExamples.q: Explain why counter-current flow in fish gills is more efficient than parallel flow.

steps.text: Blood and water start with a large gradient, but as O₂ moves into blood and CO₂ moves out, the gradient narrows — equilibrium is reached and diffusion stops (~50% extraction).
Blood always encounters water that is richer in O₂ than itself; the gradient is maintained along the entire length.
O₂ continues to diffuse into the blood along the full length → ~80% extraction efficiency.

mistakes: Describing counter-current as blood and water flowing in the same direction — they flow in OPPOSITE directions.
Forgetting that Fick's law requires surface area in the numerator AND distance in the denominator.
Stating insects use blood to carry O₂ — they don't; tracheoles carry O₂ directly to cells.
tips: Counter-current maintains the gradient — draw arrows to show directions in exam questions.
Xerophyte adaptations: always link each feature to reduced water loss.
For alveoli: state wall is one cell thick (squamous epithelium) and surrounded by capillaries.

flashcards.a: Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) / diffusion distance.

flashcards.q: How do guard cells open a stoma?
flashcards.a: Guard cells take up water by osmosis → become turgid → curved shape pulls stoma open.

flashcards.q: Why is counter-current flow more efficient than parallel flow in fish gills?
flashcards.a: Counter-current maintains a concentration gradient along the entire gill length, allowing greater O₂ extraction (~80% vs ~50%).

flashcards.q: What is the role of surfactant in the alveoli?
flashcards.a: Reduces surface tension and prevents alveoli from collapsing during expiration.

flashcards.q: How does an insect reduce water loss through spiracles?
flashcards.a: Spiracles can be closed (by valves) when gas exchange demand is low, reducing evaporation.

flashcards.q: Name four features of an efficient gas exchange surface.
flashcards.a: Large surface area; thin surface; moist; maintained concentration gradient (ventilation/blood supply).

questions.q: Which feature of alveoli minimises diffusion distance?
questions.exp: The single-celled squamous epithelium means the diffusion distance is minimised — less than 0.5 μm.

questions.q: In fish, what flow pattern maximises O₂ extraction?
questions.exp: Counter-current flow (blood and water in opposite directions) maintains a gradient along the full gill length.

questions.q: Which structure in insects controls entry of air and water loss?
questions.exp: Spiracles are openings in the exoskeleton that can be opened or closed to regulate gas entry and water loss.

questions.q: What causes a stoma to open?
opts: Guard cells become turgid and pull apart
questions.exp: Guard cells absorb water by osmosis → swell → become turgid → their curved shape pulls the pore open.

questions.q: A xerophyte has sunken stomata. How does this reduce water loss?
opts: Creates a humid microclimate in the pit, reducing the water potential gradient
questions.exp: Sunken stomata trap humid air in a pit, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient → slower evaporation.
